Question: What are your best kind of fishes?
Answer: My friend that taught me the most about fishing has 2 largemouth bass on his wall, each weighing about 10 lbs and caught in local ponds. We used to fish a good deal in fresh water lakes in Florida fishing for largemouth bass. Once, while he and I were fishing in Florida, I watched an older guy in a small Jon boat catching large bream or bluegill on a light, long fly rod. I watched with an open mouth as he landed one fish after another, most bending the rod dramatically, and I was the one hooked. That looked like such fun. So, I tend to fly fish now and prefer trout to other fish, but do enjoy panfishing and I’m not that into largemouth bass fishing, unlike most fishermen here in Georgia. Trout: These (brown, rainbow, and brook trout) are available in Georgia tailraces and in Georgia’s mountains. They regularly out-think me and are energetic fighters, jumping multiple times when hooked. Trout are gorgeous fish and live in beautiful places. Photo above from Georgia Mtn Cabins Bluegill (bream, sunfish, etc..): Bream are strong fighters and their wide bodies offer water resistance which makes for a better fight. They are easy to catch and a lot of fun. Smallmouth bass: Unlike largemouth bass, smallmouth bass run smaller than largemouth and are very vigorous fighters jumping more like a trout. From Outdoor Sports Nation Crappie: These go by many names and are referred to as slabs when they are larger. Their width, more so than even a bluegill, makes getting a crappie to hand a fun and difficult thing. They also taste great.

Question: Why do some recipes have steps that require taking food out of the oven and letting it sit? 🏋🏻‍♀️
Answer: The step you are describing is usually called “resting” and is very common when cooking meats whether they are cooked in an oven, grill or smoker, or on a stovetop (hob). A related term is “carryover cooking,” a term which applies to the redistribution of heat in foods once removed from the cooking device. There are two purposes usually attributed to the resting of foods. The first applies to most solid foods (or semi-solid like casseroles) and the second to meats. The first, carryover cooking, is to allow the thickest portion or the portion farthest from the edges to finish rising in temperature after removing it from the cooking device. The second, resting meats, has to do with re-absorbing juices into the muscle-fibers of meats. Solid and semi-solid foods vary in temperature after cooking to some degree throughout the dish. The center of a casserole might be 160F while the edges are 175F or a pork chop may be 140F in the thickest part and 165F in the thinnest. When the casserole or pork chop are rested, the higher temperatures drop with heat losses to the room and to the lower temperature sections of the dish. After resting, the center and the edges of the casserole may be both be 160F and dropping. All portions, though will have reached the desired 165F, today’s “safe-to-eat” temperature. That’s carryover cooking. The image above depicts carryover cooking. The resting period for meats is called for to reduce the amount of meat juices released once the meat is cut. During a resting period, free juices are transformed into the meat for flavor and juiciness. This resting period is more important the hotter the meat is and the larger the cut is. Normally, it is 10 minutes or more between the time a smaller cut steak or pork chop is removed from the grill and is cut as it sits on someone’s plate. The cutting also begins on a cooler edge and not in the center of the steak or chop. The juices on smaller cuts have reabsorbed by the time we cut into the center. Larger cuts, like roasts, benefit from longer resting periods. The temperature in the center takes longer to rise while resting. In fact, BBQ gurus often remove large cuts, wrap them in foil and then towels and pack them in coolers for well over an hour. This produces exceptional tenderness and flavor in my experience and in the gurus’ experiences. In the photos below, a 10 minute rest stopped all loss of juices, but not shown is that a 5 minute rest stopped almost all the loss. I can seldom get a steak off the grill and onto a plate in front of a guest in 5 minutes, so resting a small cut of meat occurs naturally. A larger cut is a very different story. Question: What is the best premixed seasoning I can buy at the store to make the best burger patties?
Answer: That’s a personal preference, but my “best” seasoning is a liquid, Dale’s Steak Seasoning. I love it on steaks, burgers, and pork chops. I used it last night (Mother’s Day) on burgers. It’s a strong seasoning and I don’t marinate with it. I just brush it on and place on the grill.

Question: What will happen if you eat bread every day?
Answer: If I eat bread every day, and I probably do, then those carbohydrates get counted toward my daily allotment of carbohydrate grams (100 g). Lately I’ve been exceeding that limit and my blood sugar readings have been a little higher. I am a diabetic and monitor my blood glucose closely. In other words, daily bread is fine for me in moderation as my carb intake is being managed. For me it’s important I eat low-insulin-stimulating bread like whole grain bread or a sourdough or a whole grain sourdough.
